A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same feature-based theory of transfer learning. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original numerical experiments with deep linear and student-teacher ReLU networks, including empirical transferability curves and comparisons with theoretical predictions.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds simulations of regularized scratch training and regularized ReLU pretraining in Appendix G.

M1.justification: v2 Figure 9 introduces a pretraining objective that penalizes hidden-weight displacement from initialization, controlling feature learning before linear transfer. This is a localized procedural addition; the original architectures, linear transfer, and full fine-tuning procedures remain.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic Gaussian-input linear regression and ablated-teacher ReLU regression. The new regularization experiments retain this coverage. Appendix C's finite-source extension is theoretical, rather than an additional empirically evaluated task or dataset.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 5 adds optimally weight-decayed scratch training alongside the original unregularized comparator. This is distinct from v1 Figure 2, which regularizes the transferred readout rather than the scratch baseline.

E3.justification: The original experimental settings remain. New Figures 5 and 9 introduce regularization sweeps over 0, 10^-4, 10^-3, 10^-2, and 10^-1, selecting models by lowest generalization error. Figure 9 fixes the retained ReLU task's ablation fraction at 0.9.

E4.justification: v2 adds two substantive diagnostic analyses: whether regularizing scratch training removes anomalous positive transfer, and whether restricting pretraining feature movement mitigates negative transfer. These directly test baseline dependence and the consequences of feature sparsification. The earlier transferred-readout ridge analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Both retain standard deviations over 20 target-dataset draws for linear experiments and the ReLU averaging descriptions involving 100 data realizations and 10 teacher or initialization draws. No changed run counts, new confidence-interval procedure, or significance testing is specified.

E6.justification: v2 adds findings that scratch regularization removes the positive-transfer spike near the interpolation threshold, while pretraining regularization substantially improves ReLU transfer at ablation fraction 0.9. These are results under added procedures. Original curves and findings, including the ReLU scaling exponent 1.18, are retained.

T1.justification: New Theorem C.1 and its Appendix D.9 proof extend fine-tuning transferability to finite, noisy source datasets and derive the modified transfer boundary. v2 also corrects the loss-decay equality in v1 Equation 48 to an upper bound in Equation 49. The dataset-distance theorem is retained as Theorem A.2.

C1.justification: The feature-space account, transferability phase diagrams, and warning about distributional distances remain. The conclusion adds a claim that pretraining between lazy and rich regimes can eliminate negative transfer, advancing regularization as a possible remedy.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses linear models' inability to capture depth-separation and nonlinear effects, qualifies anomalous transfer through its dependence on the scratch baseline, and argues for balancing lazy and rich feature learning. Appendix C additionally interprets how finite-source noise changes transfer boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository pointer in the first-page footnote and documents the new regularization penalties, grids, and model-selection rules. The original implementation settings and stopping criteria are retained, moving from Appendix D to Appendix F.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of Aminian et al. (2024), Bu et al. (2021), Ingrosso et al. (2024), and additional feature-learning and depth-separation literature; Gao and Chaudhari (2021) is removed. These broaden supporting context while retaining the central research positioning.

P1.justification: v2 revises the abstract and introduction, adds explicit contributions and an impact statement, expands the conclusion, and moves Section 2.1 into Appendix A. Terminology changes from label shift to concept drift without changing the underlying setup. Most technical exposition and the main section sequence remain.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main paper, changes header and author formatting, and substantially reflows figures. The original ridge plot moves from Figure 2 to Appendix Figure 6, and new Figures 5 and 9 are added. All seven original figures are retained.

improvement.justification: The finite-source theorem broadens the analysis, and the regularized-scratch control clarifies which transfer benefits depend on the baseline. Explicit model limitations and code-access information improve transparency. These strengthen the retained account, although Figure 9's selection by lowest generalization error limits its evidence for a practical tuning procedure.
